title: Burst attenuator: token-reservoir admission and KV swap strategy for high-QPS degradation avoidance
creator: Asha Patel
description: At sustained high QPS bursts we observe latency spikes and increased OOM churn on GPU nodes due to simultaneous microbatch growth and aggressive KV retention. This ticket designs and implements a two-part mitigation: a lightweight 'burst attenuator' that constrains admission using a token-reservoir with decay-aware replenishment, and a probabilistic KV-swap (hot-kv -> host-backed spill) policy to free GPU RAM non-disruptively.
background: Recent production incidents (see incident-2026-01-27) showed correlated latency p99 increases when multiple clients simultaneously ramp to 2-3x baseline QPS. The current admission controller grows microbatch windows until headroom is exhausted; KV cache then triggers abrupt evictions and memory reclamation causing stalls. Existing tickets explore thresholds and soft backpressure but do not address smooth absorption of short bursts while preserving long-tail latency.
goals: Absorb short-duration QPS bursts (<=30s) without causing p99 latency > 2x SLO
Avoid abrupt KV cache mass-evictions that block inference for >200ms
Maintain steady throughput for sustained loads by transitioning into controlled shedding rather than abrupt failures
Provide observability hooks to validate behavior in canaries before fleet-wide rollout
proposed_solution: Token-reservoir admission: each node maintains a lightweight reservoir of 'burst tokens' sized by free GPU headroom and recent allocation velocity. In-flight requests draw tokens; tokens replenish at an exponential-decay rate tuned per-node based on moving-average utilization.

Gradual microbatch decay: when token store is depleted, instead of immediate rejection, accept fewer tokens per request and force target batch size down via soft signaling to requesters (increase small-request penalties for batching).

KV-swap policy: probabilistic background thread identifies cold keys (LRU-ish with access skew awareness) and offloads them to node-local host memory (or NVMe) with async fetch paths. Offloading is scheduled using a cooperative backoff so it never competes aggressively with serving threads.
Admission priorities: requests carry priority hints (internal/paid/standard). The reservoir enforces per-priority weighting so critical traffic retains access during attenuation.
Fallback modes: when node-level spill + token-reservoir cannot regain headroom, trigger cross-node routing to warm standby model variants or lower-quantization variants to preserve availability.
tradeoffs: Pros: smoother latency behavior during bursts, fewer abrupt evictions, better customer experience for short spikes
Cons: additional complexity in scheduling/spill path, potential higher host-memory usage and NVMe IO; small increases in tail latency for cold-key misses after swapping
Operational trade: tuning reservoir replenish/exhaust thresholds will require phased canary testing and telemetry signals; defaults may be too permissive or too strict across different instance types
Consistency trade: KV-swap introduces a small async fetch failure mode that must be handled as transient errors; application-level semantics that expect deterministic local KV must be documented
implementation_tasks: Prototype token-reservoir in serving-runtime (C++): reservoir data-structure, draw/replenish API, per-priority weighting
Implement soft microbatch adjustment hook in admission layer to accept 'reduced batch target' flags
KV-swap: background offload worker with host-memory/NVMe persistence adapter and async fetch path in runtime
Add per-node telemetry: reservoir level, spill queue length, async-fetch miss latency, frequency of microbatch reductions
Integrate per-route priority hints via API metadata and SDK token mapping
Write unit and integration tests for race conditions in reservoir and spill path
End-to-end canary orchestration config for 1% traffic and automated rollback thresholds
metrics_and_slos: Primary guardrails: p50/p95/p99 latency on inference route (target p99 <= 2x SLO during bursts)
Reservoir saturation ratio: fraction of nodes with reservoir <=10% during 30s burst (target < 20%)
KV-spill rate: bytes/s offloaded to host per node (monitor for unbounded growth)
Async-fetch miss penalty: added latency in cold-hit path (target < 25ms median)
Customer-visible errors: 5xx rate attributable to node memory pressure (target near zero after rollout)
testing_plan: Unit tests for reservoir logic including concurrent draws and timed replenishment
Simulator load tests: synthetic multi-tenant burst generator to validate behavior across node types (A100, H100, and smaller prod GPUs)
Chaos test: introduce forced slow host-NVMe writes to ensure spill backpressure does not deadlock serving threads
Canary: deploy to 1% of traffic with automated rollback if p99 or 5xx thresholds exceeded
Post-canary long-run: 24h soak to observe steady-state KV offload and reheat behavior
decision_log: 2026-02-18: Chose token-reservoir over strict rate-limiter after simulations showed improved absorbtion of sub-30s bursts with 40% fewer rejects.
2026-02-25: Decided to implement KV-swap rather than immediate eviction to reduce blocking latencies; will use host-memory first, NVMe as fallback for capacity.
2026-03-03: Prioritization: implement reservoir + microbatch soft-reduction first (runtime-1.26); KV-swap in follow-up if canary metrics show high eviction churn

risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Host-memory or NVMe saturation if offload policy too aggressive. Mitigation: adaptive backoff in offload worker and global throttle if host usage high.
Risk: Inconsistent KV semantics for customers relying on guaranteed on-GPU cache. Mitigation: document eventual-consistency behavior and provide opt-out label to pin keys.

Risk: Reservoir tuning complexity leading to either too permissive (OOM) or too strict (unnecessary rejects). Mitigation: conservative defaults and telemetry-driven auto-tuning experiment in later cycle.
